questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Name selected non-medication first-aid supplies and distinguish their limited roles from stock/expiry/clinical-use decisions; no real kit or item inspected.
questions.prompt: Name five non-medication supplies that may appear on a first-aid kit list. Choose items for covering, securing or protection, rather than naming a medicine or a chemical to apply.
questions.answer: Examples are sterile dressing pads, adhesive plasters, roller bandages, medical adhesive tape and disposable examination gloves.
questions.explanation: These are selected supply names, not a complete or compulsory kit list for a Nigerian school or permission to use them.

markingGuide.description: Names two suitable non-medication supplies. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Name selected non-medication first-aid supplies and distinguish their limited roles from stock/expiry/clinical-use decisions; no real kit or item inspected.
questions.prompt: A paper list puts a sterile dressing pad and a roller bandage under exactly the same role. Distinguish their usual roles without placing either item on a person.
questions.answer: A dressing pad is used to cover/protect a wound surface; a roller bandage can secure a dressing. Naming their roles does not demonstrate correct treatment or application.
questions.explanation: The conceptual distinction is supported by the kit-table categories; no pressure, wrapping or clinical procedure is taught.

markingGuide.description: Explains the dressing pad’s covering/protecting role. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Explains the bandage’s securing role as distinct. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Name selected non-medication first-aid supplies and distinguish their limited roles from stock/expiry/clinical-use decisions; no real kit or item inspected.
questions.prompt: A fictional stock record lists “sterile dressing pads: expiry date passed”. A pupil says the pads must still be suitable because the packet has the right name. What should a responsible adult check or arrange, and why is the name alone insufficient?
questions.answer: The adult should check the stock information and arrange appropriate replacement/disposal of expired items. An item name does not establish that its present condition and expiry meet requirements.
questions.explanation: Only a paper stock record is considered; pupils neither inspect real sterile packs nor decide that an item is clinically safe.

markingGuide.description: Requires responsible stock checking/replacement of expired items. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.prompt: Two first-aid lists have different contents because they were prepared for different settings. Must one universal list fit every setting? Explain how a responsible adult should use the setting’s needs when planning supplies.
questions.answer: No. Supplies should reflect the assessed first-aid needs and appropriate local arrangements; a list for one setting is not automatically the complete list for another.
questions.explanation: The reference is UK workplace guidance used only for the needs-assessment principle, not Nigerian law or a child’s authority to stock a clinical kit.

markingGuide.description: Rejects a universal complete list for every setting. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Describe selected protective-barrier purposes, hand-hygiene and training limits from first-aid guidance; no PPE fitting, clinical care or practical demonstration.
questions.prompt: In a first-aid lesson, disposable examination gloves are called a protective barrier. Explain what they help reduce contact with and why that is different from healing an injury.
questions.answer: They can reduce direct contact with bodily fluids or contamination. They do not themselves heal a wound or replace appropriate care.
questions.explanation: A barrier’s purpose is explained without pupil glove use, bodily fluids or an actual injury.

markingGuide.description: Explains reduced direct contact/exposure. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Distinguishes protection from healing/treatment. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Describe selected protective-barrier purposes, hand-hygiene and training limits from first-aid guidance; no PPE fitting, clinical care or practical demonstration.
questions.prompt: A fictional first-aider’s written plan says gloves make hand hygiene unnecessary. Explain why the plan should still include appropriate hand hygiene as well as suitable protective equipment.
questions.answer: Gloves and hand hygiene are separate parts of reducing contamination risk. Hand cleaning is still needed around care and equipment handling; the glove barrier does not make hands automatically clean.
questions.explanation: This tests the relationship between measures, not a handwashing or glove-removal demonstration.

markingGuide.description: Rejects gloves as a substitute for hand hygiene. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Explains the complementary contamination-risk roles. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.learningObjective: Describe selected protective-barrier purposes, hand-hygiene and training limits from first-aid guidance; no PPE fitting, clinical care or practical demonstration.
questions.prompt: A paper protective-equipment chart lists gloves and eye protection for a trained responder facing a relevant splash hazard. Compare which areas they protect and explain why the choice must fit the hazard.
questions.answer: Gloves cover the hands, while suitable eye protection shields the eyes. Protection must address the possible exposure; protecting hands alone does not protect every part of the responder.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Describe selected protective-barrier purposes, hand-hygiene and training limits from first-aid guidance; no PPE fitting, clinical care or practical demonstration.
questions.prompt: Why should first-aid training teach how protective equipment is put on, removed and disposed of, instead of merely giving a learner a list of equipment names? Do not describe a procedure or demonstrate it.
questions.answer: Knowing a name does not ensure correct use. Incorrect handling or removal can undermine the intended barrier and spread contamination, so practical instruction and assessment are separate needs.
questions.explanation: The reference includes safe PPE handling in first-aid education; this written answer does not satisfy that training or practical skill.

markingGuide.description: Distinguishes knowing names from correct practical use. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected medicinal-drug and alcohol concepts and the protective purpose of education, without medicine decisions, personal disclosure or actual substances.
questions.prompt: In a medicine lesson, explain two legitimate purposes for which a drug may be used under appropriate care. Why is “drug” not simply another word for “something always bad”?
questions.answer: Drugs may be used to prevent or treat disease, diagnose a condition or relieve symptoms. Appropriate medical uses exist, although medicines can cause harm if unsuitable or misused.
questions.explanation: The medical meaning is distinguished from a moral label; no personal medicine choice or treatment is recommended.

markingGuide.description: Gives one legitimate medical purpose. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Gives a second distinct purpose. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Rejects an always-bad definition without claiming all use is harmless. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Explain selected medicinal-drug and alcohol concepts and the protective purpose of education, without medicine decisions, personal disclosure or actual substances.
questions.prompt: A fictional display lists alcohol separately from drugs and claims alcohol cannot affect brain function because it is found in drinks. Correct the claim using the checked meaning of alcohol.
questions.answer: Alcohol is a drug that can slow brain activity and affect functions such as judgment and coordination. Being in a drink does not remove those effects.
questions.explanation: This concerns alcohol as a substance, not beverage brands, tasting, legal ages or a safe amount for children.

markingGuide.description: Identifies alcohol as a drug. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.
Explains that a drink form does not remove its effects on brain/body function. Accept equivalent accurate age-appropriate wording.

questions.prompt: What is a useful purpose of drug and alcohol education for pupils? Explain why a lesson can teach knowledge and help-seeking without asking anyone to try a substance or disclose family use.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education

questions.prompt: In a fictional story, a child finds an unidentified pill-shaped item. Another child suggests tasting it to decide whether it is medicine or a sweet. State a safer decision and explain why appearance is not enough.
questions.answer: Do not taste or take it, and tell a responsible adult. Medicines can resemble sweets, so shape/colour is not a reliable way for a child to decide what it is.
questions.explanation: The item exists only in a story; there is no real pill, identification exercise, handling, disposal or poisoning-treatment instruction.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Classify caffeine as a stimulant and alcohol as a depressant from checked concepts, distinguishing pharmacological grouping from mood/safety and from an exhaustive taxonomy of medicines.
questions.prompt: Classify the named substances caffeine and alcohol using the selected headings stimulant and depressant. Explain the main nervous-system distinction behind those headings.
questions.answer: Caffeine is classified as a stimulant; alcohol as a depressant. The headings describe speeding up versus slowing down central nervous-system activity in the selected examples.
questions.explanation: This is a limited educational classification, not a complete account of every effect, dose or drug category. No substance is consumed.

questions.prompt: A pupil says the term depressant must mean a substance always makes every person feel sad. Explain why this is not the meaning used when alcohol is classified as a depressant.

questions.subject: Physical and Health Education
questions.learningObjective: Classify caffeine as a stimulant and alcohol as a depressant from checked concepts, distinguishing pharmacological grouping from mood/safety and from an exhaustive taxonomy of medicines.
questions.prompt: A two-column lesson chart contains only stimulant and depressant examples. A pupil says this proves that every medicine must fit exactly one of the two columns. Explain why the chart cannot support that claim, and what to do with a medicine whose effects are not supplied.
questions.answer: The chart is a selected subset, not an exhaustive or always-exclusive classification of all drugs. Without relevant information, do not guess the medicine’s class or change its use; seek appropriate information through a responsible adult or qualified professional.
questions.explanation: The primary reference recognises more grouping approaches and overlapping effects; no additional real substances, medicine decisions or complete pharmacology taxonomy are assessed.
